headline: Healey's first Budget scraps gas standing charges and doubles the bank surcharge to 6%

terms.meaning: A fixed daily fee on an energy bill, paid whatever you use.
An extra tax on banks' profits, on top of normal corporation tax.
The return investors get on UK government bonds; it shows the cost of government borrowing.

levels.headline: Healey's first Budget scraps gas standing charges and doubles the bank surcharge to 6%
levels.body:
Chancellor John Healey delivered his first Budget on 28 October, abolishing standing charges on gas bills for around 23 million homes and raising the bank corporation tax surcharge from 3% to 6% for 15 months from 1 January 2027 to 31 March 2028.
The government says the surcharge will raise £1.5 billion to help fund household and business support. The Budget speech also promised a £100 winter payment for 20 million households in council tax bands A to D. Healey said there would be no tax rises on wages or dividends.
The Office for Budget Responsibility upgraded its growth forecast to 1.2% this year, then 1% next year. But debt interest costs are £14 billion higher this year, and headroom against the government's fiscal rules is £9 billion lower than in March.
The yield on the 10-year gilt fell about 2 basis points to 5.323% as Healey spoke, a broadly positive market reaction.
levels.why: It shows how the government is paying for energy support while borrowing costs stay high.

levels.headline: Healey's first Budget removes gas standing charges and raises the bank surcharge
levels.body:
Chancellor John Healey used his first Budget on 28 October to scrap standing charges on gas bills, which affects around 23 million homes, and to double the surcharge on bank profits from 3% to 6% for 15 months from January 2027.
Ministers say the surcharge will bring in £1.5 billion towards support for households and businesses, including a £100 winter payment for 20 million households in council tax bands A to D. Healey promised no tax rises on wages or dividends.
The official forecaster, the OBR, now expects growth of 1.2% this year and 1% next year. Yet higher interest on government debt, up £14 billion this year, has cut the room for manoeuvre by £9 billion compared with March.
Government bond yields dipped slightly as the Chancellor spoke, suggesting investors were broadly comfortable.
levels.why: The Budget tries to ease winter bills without raising taxes on workers, but the public finances remain tight.

levels.headline: Budget cuts energy costs for homes and taxes banks more
levels.body:
John Healey, the Chancellor, set out his first Budget on 28 October. It removes standing charges, the fixed daily fees on gas bills, for around 23 million homes. The cost is partly covered by a bigger tax on banks.
The bank surcharge goes from 3% to 6% for 15 months from January 2027, raising an expected £1.5 billion. There will also be a £100 payment this winter for 20 million households in council tax bands A to D.
Healey said wages and dividends will not face higher taxes. The Office for Budget Responsibility expects the economy to grow 1.2% this year. However, the government is spending £14 billion more on debt interest, which leaves less spare money for future plans.
Bond markets reacted calmly, with borrowing costs edging down.
levels.why: Many households will see lower fixed energy costs, while banks face a bigger tax bill.

levels.headline: Chancellor scraps gas standing charges and taxes banks more in first Budget
levels.body:
Chancellor John Healey has delivered his first Budget, promising help with energy bills and paying for part of it by taxing banks more.
Standing charges, the fixed daily amount on a gas bill, will go for around 23 million homes. Instead, those costs will be added to the price of each unit of gas used. The bank surcharge will double from 3% to 6% for 15 months from January 2027 and is expected to raise £1.5 billion. A £100 winter payment is planned for 20 million households in council tax bands A to D.
Healey said there would be no tax rises on wages or dividends. The official forecast for growth this year is 1.2%. But the government now pays £14 billion more in debt interest, so it has less room to spend.
levels.why: It affects what families pay to heat their homes this winter.

levels.headline: Budget: gas standing charges to go, banks to pay more tax
levels.body:
Chancellor John Healey has announced his first Budget. The main aim is to help families with energy bills this winter.
A standing charge is a fixed fee you pay each day for a gas supply, even if you use none. The Budget removes it for around 23 million homes, and the cost moves into the price of the gas itself. There will also be a £100 payment for 20 million households in council tax bands A to D.
To help pay, banks will pay a higher extra tax on their profits. It rises from 3% to 6% for 15 months from January 2027 and should raise £1.5 billion. Healey said he would not raise taxes on wages or dividends.
The government is also paying £14 billion more in interest on its debts this year, which limits what it can spend.
levels.why: It could lower fixed costs on household energy bills, but the government still has little spare money.

levels.headline: Budget helps with energy bills and makes banks pay more
levels.body:
The Chancellor, John Healey, has set out the government's plans for taxes and spending. This is called the Budget.
Gas bills have a fixed daily fee called a standing charge. You pay it even if you use no gas. The Budget ends this fee for around 23 million homes. The cost will be added to the price of the gas people use instead. There will also be a £100 payment this winter for 20 million households in council tax bands A to D.
Banks will pay more tax on their profits for a while. The extra tax goes from 3% to 6% and should raise £1.5 billion. Healey said workers will not pay higher taxes on wages.
The government also owes a lot of money and must pay interest on it, now £14 billion more than before.
levels.why: It changes how some household bills are charged and who pays for the help.

levels.headline: The Budget: help with gas bills, and a bigger tax for banks
levels.body:
Every year the Chancellor says how the government will raise and spend money. This year the Chancellor is John Healey, and he spoke on 28 October.
One big change is to gas bills. Most bills include a fixed daily fee, called a standing charge, which you pay even if you use no gas. It is going for around 23 million homes. Another is a £100 payment this winter for 20 million households in council tax bands A to D. Council tax bands sort homes by value.
The money comes partly from banks. They will pay a bigger extra tax, 6% instead of 3%, for 15 months. That should raise £1.5 billion. Healey said taxes on wages will not go up.
The government borrows money too, and the interest it pays has risen by £14 billion this year.
levels.why: It affects the bills families pay to keep warm.

levels.headline: A big plan for money: help with heating bills
levels.body:
Once a year, the person in charge of the government's money explains the plan. This person is the Chancellor. This year it is John Healey.
He said gas bills will change. At the moment many bills have a fixed fee each day, even if you use no gas. That fee is called a standing charge. It will end for around 23 million homes. Some families will also get £100 this winter to help with heating.
Where does the money come from? Banks will pay more tax. A tax is money people and firms pay to the government. Banks will pay twice as much extra tax for a while, 6% instead of 3%. That should raise £1.5 billion.
The government also owes money and pays interest on it. That bill has grown by £14 billion.
levels.why: It could make heating a home cheaper for many families this winter.

levels.headline: The government has a plan to help with heating bills
levels.body:
The Chancellor looks after the country's money. His name is John Healey. He has made a plan for the year.
Many homes pay a fixed fee for gas each day. It does not matter how much gas they use. This fee will stop. Around 23 million homes will not pay it. Some families will also get £100 this winter to help pay for heat.
The government needs money to pay for this. It will ask banks to pay more tax. Tax is money that firms and people give to the government. Banks will pay a bit more for just over a year. That will raise £1.5 billion.
The government also borrowed money before. It has to pay a fee called interest for borrowing. That fee is now bigger.
levels.why: It may help families keep their homes warm.

levels.headline: Helping families stay warm
levels.body:
Imagine your class has a money jar. A grown-up called the Chancellor decides how it is used. His name is John Healey.
He said families should pay less for heating. Some bills have a daily fee, like paying to enter a shop before you buy anything. That fee will stop for gas in around 23 million homes. Some families will also get £100 this winter.
To fill the jar, banks will pay more tax. Tax is money shared to pay for things everyone uses. The banks will pay a bit more for just over a year, and that should bring in £1.5 billion.
The country has also borrowed money, a bit like borrowing pocket money. It must pay a little extra for that, and the extra has grown.
levels.why: It is meant to help families keep warm without the government spending money it has not got.

headline: Wall Street falls sharply as tech shares sink: S&P 500 down 1.82% to 7,580.07

terms.meaning: An index that tracks the share prices of 500 of the biggest companies listed in the United States.
An index dominated by technology companies, so it moves more when tech shares rise or fall.
An index of 30 large US companies, one of the oldest measures of the stock market.

levels.headline: Wall Street falls sharply as tech shares sink: S&P 500 down 1.82% to 7,580.07
levels.body:
Wall Street fell sharply on Friday 30 October, the last completed trading session, as a sell-off in technology shares deepened. The S&P 500 closed down 1.82% at 7,580.07. The Nasdaq Composite lost 2.86% to end at 25,437.00, its worst day since June, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 572.25 points, or 1.09%, to 51,770.31.
CNBC linked the selling to doubts over whether huge spending on artificial intelligence will pay off. It followed Alphabet's worst day on record on Thursday, when its shares fell about 13% and lost roughly $500 billion in value after a weak earnings report. AMD fell close to 11% and Intel about 25% on weak revenue guidance. Selling grew in the afternoon as investors took money off the table before month-end and before the US midterm elections on 3 November.
For October as a whole the Nasdaq fell 5.3%, its steepest monthly drop since March 2025. The S&P 500 lost 0.9% and the Dow gained 1.7%. Investors moved towards steadier sectors such as consumer staples and healthcare. The S&P 500 is still only a few percent below its record high.
levels.why: Share prices affect pensions, savings and company investment, and a sharp fall in tech shows how nervous investors are about AI.

levels.headline: US stocks drop as tech sell-off deepens, with the S&P 500 down 1.82%
levels.body:
US shares fell hard on Friday 30 October, the latest completed session, as investors dumped technology stocks. The S&P 500 closed down 1.82% at 7,580.07, the Nasdaq lost 2.86% to 25,437.00, and the Dow slipped 572.25 points, or 1.09%, to 51,770.31. It was the Nasdaq's worst day since June.
The main worry is whether the very large sums being spent on artificial intelligence will bring enough profit. Alphabet, Google's owner, had its worst day ever on Thursday, falling about 13% and losing around $500 billion of value after disappointing results. On Friday AMD dropped nearly 11% and Intel about 25% after weak revenue guidance, which is a company's forecast of future sales.
Selling picked up in the afternoon as traders cashed in gains before the end of the month and ahead of the US midterm elections on 3 November. Over October the Nasdaq fell 5.3%, its biggest monthly fall since March 2025, while the S&P 500 lost 0.9% and the Dow rose 1.7%. Money moved into defensive sectors like healthcare.
levels.why: It shows how worries about AI spending can quickly drag down the whole market.

levels.headline: Wall Street slides as investors dump tech shares, S&P 500 closes down 1.82%
levels.body:
Wall Street ended Friday 30 October sharply lower, the last completed trading day, after another wave of selling in technology companies. The S&P 500 index fell 1.82% to close at 7,580.07. The tech-heavy Nasdaq dropped 2.86% to 25,437.00, its worst day since June, and the Dow lost 572.25 points, or 1.09%, to finish at 51,770.31.
Investors are increasingly asking whether the vast amounts that big tech firms are spending on artificial intelligence will earn their money back. The doubts grew after Alphabet's shares fell about 13% on Thursday, the biggest one-day fall since it floated in 2004, wiping out about $500 billion. On Friday chip makers AMD and Intel both fell sharply, Intel by about 25% after giving weak guidance on sales.
Traders also sold into the end of the month and ahead of the midterm elections on 3 November. The Nasdaq lost 5.3% in October, its worst month since March 2025. The Dow, which holds fewer tech firms, rose 1.7% for the month, and the S&P 500 fell 0.9%.
levels.why: Falling share prices can hit pension pots and make firms more cautious about hiring and investing.

levels.headline: Tech sell-off drags Wall Street lower, with the S&P 500 down 1.82%
levels.body:
US stock markets fell sharply on Friday 30 October, the most recent full trading day, as investors sold technology shares. The S&P 500 closed down 1.82% at 7,580.07, the Nasdaq dropped 2.86% to 25,437.00 and the Dow fell 572.25 points, or 1.09%, to 51,770.31.
It was the Nasdaq's worst day since June. Investors are worried that the huge sums spent on artificial intelligence may not bring in enough profit. Google's owner Alphabet fell about 13% on Thursday after weak results, its worst day on record and a loss of roughly $500 billion in value. Chip firms were hit on Friday, with AMD down nearly 11% and Intel down about 25% after it gave a weak forecast.

levels.why: Big falls in shares matter to anyone with a pension or investments, and can make companies more cautious.

levels.headline: US shares fall sharply as investors sell tech companies
levels.body:
Share prices in the United States fell sharply on Friday 30 October, the last full day of trading. The S&P 500, an index that follows 500 big US companies, closed down 1.82% at 7,580.07. The Nasdaq, which has many tech firms, dropped 2.86% to 25,437.00, and the Dow, which tracks 30 large firms, fell 1.09% to 51,770.31.

levels.why: It shows how nervous investors are about AI, which can affect savings, pensions and jobs.

levels.headline: US shares fall as investors sell off tech companies
levels.body:
Share prices in the United States fell a lot on Friday 30 October. Shares are small parts of companies that people can buy and sell. The S&P 500, which follows 500 large firms, fell 1.82% to 7,580.07. The Nasdaq, full of tech firms, fell 2.86%, its worst day since June. The Dow, which follows 30 big firms, fell 1.09%.
Many investors are now worried about artificial intelligence, or AI. Big tech firms are spending huge amounts on it, and people are not sure it will make enough money. Some traders also sold shares before the month ended and before the US elections on 3 November. In October the Nasdaq fell 5.3%, its worst month since March 2025. The market is still not far below its highest level. Falls like this can affect people's pensions and savings.
levels.why: Falling shares can shrink pensions and savings, and make firms spend and hire less.

levels.headline: Share prices in the US fall a lot as tech firms are sold
levels.body:
Share prices in the United States dropped a lot on Friday 30 October. A share is a small piece of a company. People buy shares hoping the company does well. When many people sell at once, prices fall.
The S&P 500, a list of 500 big US companies, fell 1.82%. The Nasdaq, which has lots of tech firms, fell 2.86%. That was its worst day since June. The Dow, a list of 30 large companies, fell 1.09%.
Investors are worried about artificial intelligence, or AI. Big tech firms are spending a huge amount of money on it. People now ask if the firms will earn that money back. Alphabet, the company that owns Google, lost about 13% of its value on Thursday. It was the worst day in its history.
Some people also sold shares before the end of the month and before US elections on 3 November. Over October the Nasdaq fell 5.3%. Falls like this can make pensions and savings worth less.
levels.why: Many people's pensions and savings are invested in shares, so big falls can affect them.

levels.headline: US share prices fall a lot on Friday as tech firms lose value
levels.body:
On Friday 30 October, share prices in the United States fell a lot. A share is a tiny slice of a company. If you own a share, you own a little bit of that company. The price goes up and down every day, depending on how many people want to buy it.
On Friday, many people wanted to sell. The S&P 500, which follows 500 big companies, fell by 1.82%. The Nasdaq, which follows many tech companies, fell by 2.86%. The Dow, which follows 30 large companies, fell by 1.09%.
People are worried about artificial intelligence, or AI. Big tech firms are spending lots of money on it. Some people think they might not get that money back. Alphabet, the company that owns Google, lost about 13% of its value on Thursday. That has never happened to it before.
It matters because lots of pension funds own shares. When prices fall, the money saved for later is worth less, at least for now.
levels.why: It matters because many people's pensions are invested in shares.

levels.headline: Share prices fall in America and tech companies lose the most
levels.body:
Share prices fell in America on Friday 30 October. A share is a small piece of a company. People buy shares, and the price goes up or down. On Friday the prices went down, and quite a lot.
Think of a school sale where everyone wants to buy a toy. The price goes up. Now think of everyone wanting to sell the toy. The price goes down. That is what happened to tech company shares.
Tech companies make things like phones, computers and websites. Many are spending a lot of money on a new thing called artificial intelligence, or AI. Some people worry the companies will not make that money back. Google's owner, Alphabet, lost about a seventh of its value on Thursday.
Lots of ordinary people's pensions are tied up in shares. So when prices fall, adults pay attention. The prices are still not far from their highest ever, and they can rise again.
levels.why: When share prices fall, money saved for people's pensions can be worth less.

levels.headline: Share prices fell and some big companies lost a lot of money
levels.body:
On Friday, many share prices fell in America. A share is like one slice of a very big pizza. The pizza is a company. If you own a slice, you own a tiny bit of the company.
Each day, people buy and sell slices. If lots of people want a slice, the price goes up. If lots of people want to sell, the price goes down. On Friday, lots of people sold slices of technology companies. Those are companies that make computers, phones and clever robots called AI.
Some grown-ups are worried. These companies are spending a huge amount of money on AI. They are not sure they will get the money back. Think of spending all your pocket money on a toy and then not being sure you will like it.
When the prices go down, people feel worried. But prices go up and down all the time, like a seesaw in the playground.
levels.why: Share prices go up and down, and grown-ups with savings pay close attention to them.

headline: Burnham meets Scottish and Welsh leaders in Glasgow and agrees a policy sprint with Scotland

terms.meaning: Passing decision-making powers from the UK government to Scotland, Wales, Northern Ireland or local areas.
A forum where the Prime Minister meets other leaders to discuss the economy.
A group of firms, universities and researchers in one area working in the same industry.

levels.headline: Burnham meets Scottish and Welsh leaders in Glasgow and agrees a policy sprint with Scotland
levels.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham held the first National Economic Council for the nations in Glasgow on 30 October, meeting Scotland's First Minister John Swinney and Wales's First Minister Rhun ap Iorwerth, with Northern Ireland also represented. His message was "work with me to empower every single part of the UK". He said the aim was to go deeper within each nation to empower places and communities, rather than only moving powers between parliaments.
After meeting Mr Swinney, the two governments agreed a policy sprint led by No10 North, involving officials from both. The government says a second Scottish independence referendum is off the table, as the Prime Minister has repeatedly made clear.
Mr Burnham also pointed to £1 billion through UK Research and Innovation over four years for innovation clusters in the Industrial Strategy's priority sectors. In a speech on 16 October he said ministers were looking at devolving innovation, enterprise and employability funding. It is not yet clear how the money will be split between regions.
levels.why: It shows how the new Prime Minister wants to share economic power with Scotland, Wales and English regions.

levels.headline: Burnham offers devolved governments a partnership at the first nations Economic Council
levels.body:
Andy Burnham convened the first National Economic Council for the nations in Glasgow on 30 October, alongside Scottish First Minister John Swinney and Welsh First Minister Rhun ap Iorwerth, with Northern Ireland represented. The Prime Minister told the devolved governments to "work with me to empower every single part of the UK", describing his approach as going deeper within nations rather than simply shifting powers between parliaments.
Following talks with Mr Swinney, both governments agreed a policy sprint, led by No10 North and involving officials from each side. Downing Street has said a second independence referendum in Scotland is not on the table.
The Prime Minister highlighted £1 billion of funding through UKRI over four years to support innovation clusters in priority sectors. On 16 October he said the UK was considering how to devolve innovation, enterprise and employability funding to match local strengths. No breakdown of how the money will be divided has been published.
levels.why: The approach could change how money and decisions flow between Westminster, the nations and English regions.

levels.headline: PM tells devolved governments to 'work with me' as the nations' Economic Council meets in Glasgow
levels.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham met the First Ministers of Scotland and Wales in Glasgow on 30 October for the first National Economic Council aimed at the nations, with Northern Ireland also represented. He said he wanted to "empower every single part of the UK", and to push power further down to local places and communities, instead of just moving it from one parliament to another.
After talks with Scotland's John Swinney, the two governments agreed a policy sprint, a short and focused piece of joint work led by the No10 North team. The UK government says a new Scottish independence referendum is not on offer.
Mr Burnham also pointed to £1 billion over four years, channelled through UK Research and Innovation, for innovation clusters. These are areas where businesses, universities and researchers work together in industries the government wants to grow. Plans to hand regions more control over innovation and jobs funding are being looked at, but the split of cash is unclear.
levels.why: It shows whether the government can share economic power across the UK without reopening the independence row.

levels.headline: Burnham offers Scotland and Wales a partnership at first nations Economic Council
levels.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham met Scotland's First Minister John Swinney and Wales's First Minister Rhun ap Iorwerth in Glasgow on 30 October for the first National Economic Council for the nations. Northern Ireland was also represented. Mr Burnham urged them to "work with me to empower every single part of the UK" and said power should move deeper into communities, not just between parliaments.
Afterwards, the UK and Scottish governments agreed a policy sprint, a short burst of joint work led by No10 North. Another independence referendum in Scotland is off the table, the Prime Minister has said.
He also pointed to £1 billion over four years through UK Research and Innovation for innovation clusters, which are groups of firms and researchers in the same industry. He has said the government is looking at devolving funding for innovation, enterprise and employability, meaning help into work. How the cash will be shared out has not been set out.
levels.why: It could decide how much say Scotland, Wales and English regions have over their own economies.

levels.headline: PM meets Scottish and Welsh leaders and offers to share more power
levels.body:
The Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, met the leaders of Scotland and Wales in Glasgow on 30 October. John Swinney is Scotland's First Minister and Rhun ap Iorwerth is Wales's. Northern Ireland also sent a representative. It was the first time a new group called the National Economic Council met for the nations.
Mr Burnham asked them to "work with me" so that every part of the UK has more say over its own future. He wants power to go down to towns, cities and regions, not only to move between the parliaments in London, Edinburgh and Cardiff.
The UK and Scottish governments agreed to do a short, focused piece of joint work called a policy sprint. The government says there will not be another vote on Scottish independence.
Mr Burnham also pointed to £1 billion over four years to help groups of firms and researchers grow new industries. It is not yet clear how the money will be shared.
levels.why: It affects who makes decisions about jobs, funding and local services across the UK.

levels.headline: The Prime Minister meets Scottish and Welsh leaders and offers to share power
levels.body:
On 30 October the Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, travelled to Glasgow to meet the leaders of Scotland and Wales, John Swinney and Rhun ap Iorwerth. Northern Ireland also sent a representative. Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland each have their own government, which makes many decisions locally. This is called devolution.
Mr Burnham said he wants to work with them so that every part of the UK has a real say. He also wants cities, towns and regions to get more control, not just the nations.
The Scottish and UK governments agreed to carry out a short piece of joint work, called a policy sprint. The UK government says there will not be a second vote on Scottish independence.
The Prime Minister also spoke about £1 billion over four years to help local businesses and researchers grow new industries. It has not yet been said how the money will be shared out between different areas.
levels.why: It could change who decides how money is spent on jobs and services near you.

levels.headline: The Prime Minister meets Scottish and Welsh leaders to share power
levels.body:
On 30 October the Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, met leaders from Scotland and Wales in the city of Glasgow. The leaders are called First Ministers. They run the Scottish and Welsh governments, which look after things like health and schools in their own countries. This idea is called devolution.
Mr Burnham said he wanted to "work with" them so that every part of the UK has more say. He also wants power to go down to local areas, such as cities and towns.
The Scottish and UK governments agreed to do a short, focused piece of work together, called a policy sprint. The government says there will not be another vote on whether Scotland should become independent.
The Prime Minister also talked about £1 billion over four years. It is to help businesses, universities and researchers in the same area to grow new industries and create jobs. We do not yet know how the money will be shared.
levels.why: It could change who decides how money is spent on jobs and services where you live.

levels.headline: The Prime Minister meets leaders of Scotland and Wales in Glasgow
levels.body:
On 30 October the Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, met two leaders in a city called Glasgow. They were John Swinney, who leads the Scottish government, and Rhun ap Iorwerth, who leads the Welsh government. Scotland and Wales make many of their own rules, for example about hospitals and schools.
The Prime Minister said he wants to "work with" them. He wants every part of the UK to have more say about its own future. He also wants towns and cities to be able to make more choices themselves.
The Scottish government and the UK government agreed to do a short, focused piece of work together. It is called a policy sprint. The government says there will not be another vote on Scotland leaving the UK.
The Prime Minister also talked about £1 billion over four years. It will help local businesses and scientists grow new industries. Nobody has said yet how it will be shared out.
levels.why: It could change who decides how money is spent in your area.

levels.headline: The Prime Minister wants to share more power with Scotland and Wales
levels.body:
The Prime Minister is the person in charge of the UK government. His name is Andy Burnham. On 30 October he went to a city in Scotland called Glasgow. He met the leaders of Scotland and Wales. Each country has its own government, and they make some of their own rules.
Mr Burnham said he wants to work as a team with them. He wants every part of the UK to have a say in what happens near them. It is a bit like a class teacher letting different groups choose how they will do a project.
The Scottish government and the UK government agreed to do some quick, shared work. The government also said Scotland will not have another vote on becoming its own country.
He also talked about £1 billion of money. It would help new businesses and scientists. We do not know yet who will get how much.
levels.why: It might change who makes choices about things near where you live.

levels.headline: The Prime Minister met leaders from Scotland and Wales to work as a team
levels.body:
The UK has four parts. They are England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. The Prime Minister is the person who leads the whole UK. This week he went to Glasgow, a big city in Scotland, to meet the leaders of Scotland and Wales.
Think of it like a school team. The captain, who is the Prime Minister, wants every player to have a say. He said he wants to work with them, not boss them around. He wants towns and cities to have more say too.
The Scottish leader and the Prime Minister agreed to do some quick work together. They will try to find ideas that help people in Scotland.
The Prime Minister also talked about a big pot of money, £1 billion. It would help new businesses and scientists. Nobody knows yet how the money will be shared out.
levels.why: The grown-ups are deciding who gets to make choices about things near you.

headline: UK inflation jumps to 3.5% as markets expect the Bank of England to raise rates on 5 November

terms.meaning: The rate at which prices rise over time.
Inflation leaving out food and energy, which swing a lot.
The Bank of England's main interest rate, which influences mortgage and savings rates.

levels.headline: UK inflation jumps to 3.5% as markets expect the Bank of England to raise rates on 5 November
levels.body:
UK consumer price inflation rose to 3.5% in the 12 months to September, up from 3.1% in August and above the 3.4% economists expected. Core inflation, which strips out food and energy, rose to 2.8% from 2.6%.
Fuel was the main driver, with motor fuel prices up 29.8% on a year earlier. Services inflation has also quickened, which analysts read as a sign that higher energy costs are feeding through to the wider economy.
The Bank of England's benchmark Bank Rate is 3.75%, against a 2% inflation target. Markets strongly expect a rise at the next meeting on 5 November, which would be the first since 2023, and one note said traders had priced in at least three quarter-point rises by April 2027.
The Budget forecasts say inflation will peak at 3.8% in early 2027.
levels.why: Higher rates would raise borrowing costs for mortgage holders and businesses.

levels.headline: Inflation rises to 3.5% and a Bank of England rate rise looks likely next week
levels.body:
UK inflation climbed to 3.5% in September from 3.1% in August, beating forecasts of 3.4%. Core inflation, excluding food and energy, rose to 2.8% from 2.6%.
Motor fuel prices were 29.8% higher than a year earlier and were the biggest cause. Services inflation also picked up, suggesting higher energy costs are spreading through the economy.

headline: Burnham wants an 'honest discussion' on EU free movement ahead of the 20 November Brussels summit

levels.headline: Burnham wants an 'honest discussion' on EU free movement ahead of the 20 November Brussels summit
levels.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said the UK should have an "honest discussion" about how immigration has changed since Brexit, as the UK and EU prepare for a summit in Brussels on 20 November, according to Euronews reporting of a Sunday Times interview.
He has ruled out joining the euro or the Schengen travel area, and has said he is committed to the 2024 Labour manifesto, which ruled out free movement, single market membership and a customs union. No agreement on free movement has been confirmed.
On the table at the summit are a trade deal on food and drink, progress on linking emissions trading and energy systems, a youth experience scheme and deeper cooperation on immigration. The sides are far apart on youth visas: the UK has pushed for a cap below 50,000, Brussels up to 150,000. Nigel Farage called Burnham's comments a "total betrayal of Brexit Britain".
levels.why: The summit could set the UK's relationship with its biggest trading partner for years.

levels.headline: Iran says four tankers hit mines in the Strait of Hormuz as Vance tries to revive peace talks
levels.body:
Iran's Revolutionary Guard said on 29 and 30 October that three tankers caught fire after hitting naval mines on what it called an "unauthorised southern route" near the Omani coast of the Strait of Hormuz, and Iran's army said a fourth was burning east of the strait. It is unclear whether Friday's reported vessels are additional ships. The claims have not been independently confirmed, and US Central Command's Brad Cooper has repeated that the main shipping lanes have been cleared of Iranian mines.
Separately, the maritime security body UKMTO reported that a small boat attached explosives to a tanker's hull. The fire was put out, all crew were safe and no pollution was reported.
Meanwhile Vice President JD Vance sent a letter through Qatari mediators proposing a framework for talks. Trump said he had not directed it. Iran was expected to answer a revised Qatari proposal by the end of the week. Analysts fear fighting could resume after the 3 November US midterms.
levels.why: The strait carries much of the world's oil, so incidents there can push up fuel prices and risk a wider war.

headline: Israel faces weeks of coalition talks as neither Netanyahu's bloc nor Eisenkot's reaches 61 seats

levels.headline: Israel faces weeks of coalition talks as neither Netanyahu's bloc nor Eisenkot's reaches 61 seats
levels.body:

The Joint List and Ra'am won a combined 19, a record for Arab-led parties. A majority needs 61 of the 120 seats.
Turnout was around 77.7%, the highest in 27 years. President Isaac Herzog will consult parties and name the person best placed to form a government. A coalition has 28 days to form, extendable by up to 14, otherwise new elections follow, with Netanyahu staying in office meanwhile.
Likud alleges Arab-led parties "stole" the election, without evidence. The Shin Bet has been asked to investigate suspicions of improper foreign funding, which Qatar denies. Results are due to be certified by 4 November, and the new Knesset is sworn in on 10 November.
levels.why: The result decides who leads Israel during the Gaza and Iran conflicts and could force another election.

levels.why: It decides who leads Israel next and whether there will be another vote.

levels.headline: Spain train crash death toll revised to 69 as investigators examine a 'inexplicable' control centre order
levels.body:
The death toll from Wednesday's high-speed train collision near Urda in Toledo province, on the Madrid to Seville line, has been revised to 69 from the 74 first reported by the transport ministry. headline: Binance says about $6.3 billion was taken in the largest crypto theft on record

terms.meaning: A company where people buy, sell and store digital currencies such as Bitcoin.

Whether a company has enough assets to cover what it owes.

levels.headline: Binance says about $6.3 billion was taken in the largest crypto theft on record
levels.body:
The cryptocurrency exchange Binance disclosed a major security breach on 29 and 30 October, estimating that around $6.3 billion in client assets was affected. It is the largest crypto theft on record. TRM Labs put the sum moved from Binance wallets at about $6.36 billion across 10 blockchains, and Chainalysis cited $6.4 billion. Reports say roughly half has been frozen on-chain, and Binance has begun recovering assets using its Secure Asset Fund for Users, known as SAFU.
Binance first said a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop may have been involved, but co-chief executive Richard Teng later said the attack was more complex. The firm said it had found no evidence that any wallet private key had leaked.
TRM Labs attributed the attack with high confidence to TraderTraitor, a North Korean state-sponsored hacking unit, and Chainalysis reached a similar view. Neither Binance nor the FBI had confirmed that. Bitcoin fell about 4%, but analysts said the breach did not appear to pose a significant solvency risk to Binance.
levels.why: It is the biggest crypto theft ever, and shows how exposed even the largest exchanges can be to hackers.

levels.headline: Binance confirms record hack of about $6.3 billion, with roughly half frozen

Freezing coins stops them moving but does not return them: that needs a separate legal process. Bitcoin dropped about 4%, but analysts do not currently see a serious solvency threat to Binance.
levels.why: The hack could shake confidence in crypto exchanges and show the reach of state-backed hackers.

headline: Bank of Japan holds rates at 1.25% and says underlying inflation now fits its 2% target

terms.meaning: The steady rise in prices once temporary swings, such as energy costs, are set aside.
The interest rate set by a central bank, which influences borrowing costs across the economy.
The public body, such as the Bank of Japan, that manages a country's money and interest rates.

levels.headline: Bank of Japan holds rates at 1.25% and says underlying inflation now fits its 2% target
levels.body:
The Bank of Japan kept its policy rate at 1.25% on 30 October and said for the first time since it adopted the target in 2013 that underlying inflation is generally consistent with its 2% goal. Before this it had described underlying inflation as approaching 2%. The decision was 8 to 1, with board member Hajime Takata wanting a rise to 1.5%.
The bank raised its inflation forecast for fiscal 2027 to 2.6%, and its core-core forecast, which strips out fresh food and energy, to 2.7% from 2.6%. It warned that underlying inflation could run above 2% as firms shift towards raising wages and prices. September core inflation was 2.1%, the highest of 2026 and above expectations, although some experts say headline inflation is held down by energy subsidies.
The bank raised rates to 1.25% on 18 September, the highest since 1995. A CNBC survey of 16 economists found all expect another increase in December or January.
levels.why: It signals that Japan's long fight against falling prices is over, and that borrowing costs there are likely to keep rising.

levels.headline: Bank of Japan holds at 1.25% but says inflation is now in line with its target
levels.body:
The Bank of Japan left interest rates at 1.25% on 30 October and, for the first time since setting a 2% target in 2013, judged that underlying inflation was generally consistent with it. It had previously said underlying inflation was approaching the target. The vote was 8 to 1; Hajime Takata wanted to raise the rate to 1.5%.
The central bank lifted its inflation forecast for fiscal 2027 to 2.6% and its core-core measure, which excludes fresh food and energy, to 2.7%. It said inflation could overshoot 2% as companies increasingly raise wages and prices. September core inflation was 2.1%, the highest this year. Some experts argue headline inflation would be higher without energy subsidies.
Rates reached 1.25% on 18 September, the highest since 1995. All 16 economists in a CNBC poll expect another rise in December or January.
levels.why: The shift could lift Japanese borrowing costs and affect the yen and global bond markets.

levels.headline: Bank of Japan keeps rates at 1.25% and says inflation now matches its 2% goal

Japan's central bank held interest rates at 1.25% on 30 October. It said that underlying inflation, the steady rise in prices once temporary swings are set aside, is now generally consistent with its 2% target. This is the first time it has said so since it adopted the target in 2013. One of nine board members, Hajime Takata, voted to raise rates to 1.5%.
The bank raised its inflation forecast for fiscal 2027 to 2.6%, and warned prices could rise faster than 2% as firms push through higher wages and prices. September core inflation was 2.1%, the highest this year, though energy subsidies are thought to be holding down the headline figure.
Rates went up to 1.25% on 18 September, the highest since 1995. In a CNBC survey, all 16 economists expect another increase in December or January.
levels.why: Japan spent decades with weak prices, so hitting its target is a major change that could push up its interest rates.

levels.headline: Bank of Japan holds interest rates and says inflation is back at its target
levels.body:
The Bank of Japan kept interest rates at 1.25% on 30 October. It also said that the steady, underlying rise in prices is now in line with its 2% goal, for the first time since it set that goal in 2013. Eight of its nine board members voted to hold rates. One, Hajime Takata, wanted a rise to 1.5%.
The bank now expects inflation of 2.6% in fiscal 2027, higher than before. It said prices could rise by more than 2% as companies lift wages and prices together. Core inflation in September was 2.1%, the highest this year. Some experts think government help with energy bills is keeping the headline figure lower.
Japan raised rates on 18 September to their highest since 1995. A survey of 16 economists by CNBC found that all expect another rise in December or January.
levels.why: Japan had falling or flat prices for decades, so a return to 2% inflation changes how its economy works.

levels.headline: Japan's central bank holds rates but says prices are now rising as it hoped
levels.body:
Japan's central bank, the Bank of Japan, kept its main interest rate at 1.25% on 30 October. It also said that prices are now rising at the pace it wants. Its goal is 2% a year, which it set in 2013. For many years prices in Japan hardly rose, or even fell, so this is a big change.
Eight of the nine board members voted to keep the rate where it is. One member, Hajime Takata, wanted to raise it to 1.5%.
The bank thinks prices could rise 2.6% in the year to March 2028, and could rise faster than 2% if companies keep raising pay and prices. In September, core inflation was 2.1%, the highest this year.
The rate was raised to 1.25% in September, the highest since 1995. Economists in a survey all expect another rise in December or January.
levels.why: Prices rising slowly and steadily is what central banks aim for, and Japan has now reached it.

levels.headline: Bank of Japan holds rates and says prices are now rising as it wanted
levels.body:
Japan's central bank, the Bank of Japan, kept its main interest rate at 1.25% on 30 October. The interest rate is the cost of borrowing money, and the bank uses it to influence how fast prices rise. The decision was 8 to 1, with one board member, Hajime Takata, wanting a rise to 1.5%.
The bank also said that underlying inflation, the steady rise in prices once short-term swings are ignored, now fits its 2% goal. It has not said this since it set the target in 2013. For decades prices in Japan barely rose, so this is a big change.
It now expects prices to rise 2.6% in fiscal 2027, and warned they could go up faster than 2% if firms keep raising wages and prices. Core inflation in September was 2.1%, the highest this year.
Rates went up to 1.25% in September, the highest since 1995, and economists in a CNBC survey expect another rise in December or January.
levels.why: Prices rising gently is what central banks aim for, and Japan has now reached it after decades.

levels.headline: Japan's central bank keeps its rate the same and says prices are rising as planned
levels.body:
Japan's central bank is called the Bank of Japan. It decides the interest rate. That is the price of borrowing money. On 30 October it kept the rate at 1.25%. Eight of nine board members agreed. One wanted to raise it to 1.5%.
The bank also said something new. Prices are now rising as fast as it wants. Its goal is 2% more each year. In Japan, prices hardly went up for around thirty years, so this is a big change. A little inflation is normal and seen as healthy.
Prices in September were 2.1% higher than a year before, using one of the bank's main measures. The bank thinks prices might keep rising a bit faster than 2% because companies are raising pay and prices.
Economists think the bank will raise its rate again in December or January.
levels.why: Japan's prices stayed flat for years, so this change affects pay, savings and borrowing there.

levels.headline: Japan's bank keeps the cost of borrowing the same and says prices are rising as planned
levels.body:
Japan has a central bank called the Bank of Japan. It sets the cost of borrowing money. This is called the interest rate. On 30 October it kept the rate at 1.25%. Eight of the nine people on its board agreed, but one wanted it higher.
The bank also said that prices are rising by about 2% a year, as it wanted. That might sound odd, but a little rise in prices is seen as healthy. For a very long time in Japan prices stayed the same, which made it hard for the country to grow.
Prices in September were 2.1% higher than a year earlier on one main measure. Firms are also raising pay, which helps people buy things.
Experts think the bank will raise the rate again in December or January.
levels.why: It shows Japan's economy is changing after many years of flat prices.

levels.headline: Japan's money bank says prices are going up slowly, as it hoped
levels.body:
Every country has a special bank that looks after its money. In Japan, it is called the Bank of Japan. It decides how much it costs to borrow money. On 30 October it kept that cost the same.
The bank also said that prices are now going up by about 2% each year. This is the slow, steady rise that it wanted. Imagine a sweet that cost 100 yen last year and now costs 102 yen. That is a slow rise.
For a very long time in Japan, prices did not go up at all. Shops could not charge more, and workers often did not get pay rises. Now many firms are paying their workers a bit more, and prices are going up gently.
Experts think the bank may make borrowing a little more costly in the winter.
levels.why: Gently rising prices and pay are a sign that a country's economy is healthy.

levels.headline: A country's money bank says prices are rising slowly, like it wanted
levels.body:
Japan is a country far away in Asia. It has a special bank that looks after the country's money. The bank is called the Bank of Japan. It decides how much extra people must pay when they borrow money.
Think about the price of a sweet in the school shop. If it costs 100 yen one year and 102 yen the next, it has gone up a tiny bit. The bank wants prices to go up by about this much every year. It says this has now started to happen.
In Japan, prices stayed the same for a very long time. Shops could not charge more, and workers often did not get pay rises. Now some companies are paying their workers a bit more.
On Friday, the bank left the price of borrowing the same. Grown-ups think it may raise it soon.
levels.why: A little rise in prices each year is a sign of a healthy economy.

headline: European gas price crosses €100 for the first time since 2022 as the EU warns of a new energy crisis

levels.headline: European gas price crosses €100 for the first time since 2022 as the EU warns of a new energy crisis

headline: Oil stays near $115 a barrel as peace hopes offset a reported Houthi attack on a Saudi refinery

levels.headline: Oil stays near $115 a barrel as peace hopes offset a reported Houthi attack on a Saudi refinery
levels.body:
Brent crude futures fell 44 cents to settle at $114.88 a barrel on Thursday 29 October, while US West Texas Intermediate lost 78 cents to settle at $102, according to CNBC. Brent had closed at $116.72 earlier in the week, its highest settlement since 29 April.
Prices have been driven by the conflict with Iran and attacks on Saudi energy sites. Iran-allied Houthi militants said they hit Saudi Arabia's Ras Tanura refinery with a ballistic missile. Traders are also watching whether the US might take military action against Iran after the 3 November midterm elections.
On the other side, Vice President JD Vance has reportedly contacted Iran's Security Council chief, Mohsen Rezaei, to try to restart peace talks. Meanwhile the US Strategic Petroleum Reserve held 282.6 million barrels last week, its lowest since 1982.
levels.why: High oil prices feed straight into petrol, transport and food costs and raise inflation.

levels.headline: Oil eases to about $115 as peace efforts compete with fears over Saudi attacks

levels.why: Oil costs affect fuel prices and inflation in almost every country.

levels.headline: Oil prices dip but stay high as Middle East tensions continue

levels.why: Higher oil prices push up petrol costs and prices in the shops.

headline: ECB holds rates at 2.5% as Lagarde announces she will leave early in February 2027

levels.headline: ECB holds rates at 2.5% as Lagarde announces she will leave early in February 2027
levels.body:
The European Central Bank kept its deposit rate at 2.5% on 29 October, after two rate rises this year, the latest in September. Inflation across the euro area has reached 3.8%, almost double the ECB's 2% target and the highest since September 2023, driven mainly by energy costs linked to the war involving Iran.
President Christine Lagarde said the decision was unanimous but that policymakers seriously debated a rise. Markets read it as a hawkish pause, with traders pricing about a 67% chance of a quarter-point increase in December.
Lagarde also said she will leave on 7 February 2027, around nine months before her eight-year term ends, saying she cannot "remain neutral" given recent developments. Spain's Pablo Hernández de Cos and the Netherlands' Klaas Knot are seen as leading candidates to succeed her. The European Council will appoint the new president.
levels.why: The ECB's rate decisions shape borrowing costs across Europe, and its next leader will steer them.

levels.headline: ECB pauses at 2.5% while Lagarde confirms an early exit
levels.body:
The European Central Bank held its key interest rate at 2.5% on 29 October after raising rates twice this year, most recently in September. Euro area inflation is 3.8%, the highest since September 2023 and nearly double the 2% target, with energy costs the main driver.
Christine Lagarde said the decision to hold was unanimous, though a rise was seriously discussed. Traders see a pause with a bias to tighten, and price about a 67% chance of a rise in December.
Lagarde announced she will step down on 7 February 2027, some nine months before her term was due to end, saying she cannot "remain neutral". Pablo Hernández de Cos of Spain and Klaas Knot of the Netherlands are seen as frontrunners to replace her, and the European Council will make the choice.
levels.why: Changes at the top of the ECB could affect how Europe handles high inflation.

levels.headline: ECB holds interest rates and Lagarde says she will leave early
levels.body:
The European Central Bank left its main interest rate at 2.5% on 29 October. It had raised rates twice this year, the last time in September. Inflation in the euro area is 3.8%, the highest since September 2023 and well above the 2% target. High energy costs are the main cause.
President Christine Lagarde said the vote to hold was unanimous but that members seriously discussed raising rates. Investors think a rise in December is likely, giving it about a 67% chance.
Lagarde also announced she will leave on 7 February 2027, about nine months before her eight-year term ends. She said she cannot "remain neutral" given recent developments. Spain's Pablo Hernández de Cos and the Netherlands' Klaas Knot are seen as likely successors.
levels.why: Interest rates in the euro area affect loans, savings and prices for millions of people.

levels.headline: European Central Bank keeps rates at 2.5% and its president says she is leaving

The European Central Bank (ECB) kept its main interest rate at 2.5% on 29 October. It is the bank for the countries that use the euro. It raised rates twice this year to fight rising prices. Inflation there is now 3.8%, nearly double its 2% target, mostly because energy costs are high.

levels.why: The ECB's choices affect prices and borrowing costs in countries that use the euro.

levels.headline: Europe's money bank pauses and its boss will leave

Lots of countries in Europe use the same money, called the euro. A bank called the European Central Bank looks after it. On 29 October, this bank said it would not change its main interest rate. It stays at 2.5%.
Interest is the extra money you pay when you borrow, or get when you save. The bank had put the rate up twice this year, because prices were rising too fast. Prices there are going up by 3.8% a year. The bank wants only 2%. High energy costs are the main cause.
The boss, Christine Lagarde, said she will leave in February 2027. That is early. People are talking about who might replace her.
levels.why: It helps decide how much it costs to borrow money in Europe.

levels.headline: A big bank keeps its rate the same

levels.why: Its choices can change how much things cost for families in Europe.

On 29 October, the banker said the extra charge, called the interest rate, would stay at 2.5%. Prices have been going up quickly, partly because energy costs a lot. The bank wants prices to rise slowly. It may raise the charge again in December.

levels.why: It matters because the cost of borrowing touches many families.

headline: US midterms on 3 November: polls favour Democrats as Trump's economic approval hits a low

levels.headline: US midterms on 3 November: polls favour Democrats as Trump's economic approval hits a low
levels.body:
Americans vote in the midterm elections on Tuesday 3 November, and polls and forecasts point to Democratic gains. A CNBC/All-America survey of 1,000 registered voters, carried out from 14 to 18 October, found that voters preferred Democratic control of Congress by 52% to 45%. One tracker had Democrats about 9 points ahead on the generic ballot as of 28 October. The House looks more likely to flip than the Senate, where Democrats are narrowly favoured by DecisionDeskHQ. A Kalshi prediction market put the chance of a Democratic sweep of both chambers at 63%.
President Donald Trump's approval stood at 40%, with 59% disapproving. His net economic approval of minus 31 is the lowest of either of his terms. House Speaker Mike Johnson says the polling is inaccurate, but Wolfe Research says a Republican House win would need an unprecedented polling miss.
CNBC reports that Wall Street is preparing for Democratic gains. The new Congress is due to convene on 3 January.
levels.why: The result will shape what President Trump can pass for the next two years and could move markets.

levels.headline: Democrats favoured in US midterms as Trump's economic ratings fall to a record low

Mr Trump's approval is 40% against 59% disapproving, and his net economic approval of minus 31 is his lowest in either term.
Speaker Mike Johnson dismissed the polls as inaccurate, though Wolfe Research argues a Republican House win would take a miss without precedent in modern polling. Investors are preparing for a Democratic gain.
levels.why: A Democratic Congress could block parts of the president's agenda and change US policy on spending and trade.

levels.headline: Polls point to Democratic gains in the US midterm elections on 3 November

levels.why: The vote decides how much power the president has to pass laws in his last two years.

levels.headline: Americans vote on Tuesday, and polls say the president's opponents may win
levels.body:
On Tuesday 3 November, people in America will vote in elections called the midterms. They are called that because they happen in the middle of a president's four years. Voters choose members of Congress, the people who make the laws in America.
The president now is Donald Trump. He belongs to the Republican party. His main opponents are the Democrats. Polls ask people who they will vote for. In one poll, more people said Democrats than Republicans. So Democrats might win more seats.
Only 40 out of every 100 people say they like how Mr Trump is doing his job. Even fewer are happy with how he handles money and jobs.
One Republican leader says the polls are wrong. But experts say the polls would have to be very wrong for the Republicans to keep control of one part of Congress.
levels.why: The winners will help decide what laws America makes.

levels.headline: Americans vote on Tuesday to choose who makes the laws
levels.body:
On Tuesday, people in America will vote. These votes are called the midterms. They are called that because they happen in the middle of the time a president is in charge. The president is Donald Trump.
People will choose members of a group called Congress. Congress makes the laws for America, a bit like a big class council. Two big parties usually win the most seats. They are the Republicans, who are Mr Trump's party, and the Democrats, who disagree with him.
Polls ask people how they will vote. In one poll, more people said they would vote for the Democrats. So the Democrats might win more seats.
Only about four in ten people say they like how Mr Trump is doing his job. One Republican leader says the polls are wrong. Experts say they would have to be very wrong.
levels.why: The people who win will help decide what laws America has.

levels.headline: People in America will soon vote to choose their law makers
levels.body:
Soon the people of America will vote. They will choose some of the people who make the laws. Those people work in a big building called Congress. The leader of the whole country is called the president. His name is Donald Trump.
Imagine your class is choosing helpers. Some children want one helper, and some want another. Everyone votes and the one with most votes wins. In America there are two big teams, called parties. They are the Republicans and the Democrats.
Before the vote, grown-ups ask people who they plan to pick. More people said they would pick the Democrats. But asking is not the same as voting. We only find out the real answer when the votes are counted.
Mr Trump is a Republican. Fewer than half of people say they like the job he is doing.
levels.why: The winners will help decide what rules America has.
